This guide walks through a step-by-step framework for parents of 13 to 17 year olds, with a separate track for young adults aged 18 to 24.


> **Quick Answer:** To teach your teenager to invest, start with how markets work, then open a custodial or teen-owned brokerage account together. Let them research companies they already know, start with small amounts, and review results regularly. Apps like[Bloom](https://bloomapp.com/) combine real investing with structured lessons, so the learning sticks alongside the doing.


*This article is educational and does not constitute personalized financial advice. All investing involves risk, including the possible loss of principal.*


---


### Why You're the Most Important Investing Influence Your Teen Has


A 2026 survey published by Schwab found that 70% of teens aged 13 to 17 are highly interested in investing, and 73% of parents say teaching their child to invest is important. The most telling number: 56% of teens say they trust their parents most as a source of investing information — ahead of social media, school, and financial professionals.


That puts you in a stronger position than you might think. Your teen isn't tuning you out on this topic. They're waiting for you to bring it up.


The challenge most parents face isn't motivation — it's structure. You don't need to be an expert. You need a framework your teen can follow, a safe environment to make small mistakes, and tools that keep them engaged long enough for the habits to form.


---


### A Step-by-Step Framework for Teaching Your Teen to Invest


#### Step 1: Start With the "Why Money Grows" Conversation


Before any account gets opened, have a short conversation about compound growth. No charts, no spreadsheets required. Ask your teen to imagine putting money somewhere that earns a little more each year — and that extra money also earns money. Let the idea land.


The goal isn't to impress them with math. It's to make them curious. Curiosity is what keeps a teen checking their portfolio instead of forgetting it exists.


#### Step 2: Teach the Vocabulary Without the Jargon


A stock is a small ownership stake in a company. An ETF is a basket of stocks you can buy as one thing. A portfolio is just the collection of investments you own. Risk means the value can go down, not just up.


Keep definitions short and tie them to things your teen already knows. If they use a streaming service, they can own a piece of that company. If they wear a particular brand of shoes, that brand is probably publicly traded. Familiarity takes the intimidation out of it.


#### Step 3: Run a Mock Portfolio Before Real Money


Spend two to four weeks doing a paper-trading exercise. Pick five to ten companies your teen recognizes, write down the share prices, and track them weekly. Ask your teen to predict which ones will go up — and why.


This does two things formal lessons often miss: it builds intuition through observation, and it shows your teen that stock prices don't always move the way you'd expect. Both lessons hit harder when no real money is on the line.


---


### Two Action Tracks: Teens (13–17) and Young Adults (18–24)


#### Track A: Parent and Teen Together (Ages 13–17)


**Setting up the account.** Teens under 18 can't open a standard brokerage account on their own. You have two main options: a custodial account (owned by you, managed jointly) or a teen-owned account through a platform that supports minors. Bloom supports teen accounts starting at age 13, with a parent-linked custodial setup that keeps you in the loop while giving your teen real ownership of the experience.


**Start with education before execution.** Before your teen places their first trade, work through some foundational lessons together. Bloom offers more than 300 bite-sized lessons covering everything from basic market mechanics to reading a balance sheet. The app's AI assistant, Bloomie, answers questions in plain language — which is genuinely useful when your teen hits a concept that feels abstract and doesn't want to ask out loud.


**Use mirror portfolios as a teaching tool.** One of the more effective ways to introduce investing strategy without overwhelming a beginner is to show them how experienced investors actually build portfolios. Bloom lets users mirror the portfolios of well-known Wall Street investors, giving your teen a concrete example to study, compare against their own picks, and ask questions about.


**Keep position sizes small.** Fractional shares mean your teen can own a piece of a company for a few dollars. Starting small isn't about limiting upside — it's about keeping the emotional stakes manageable while the learning is happening. A teen who loses $8 on a bad pick learns the same lesson as one who loses $80, but recovers faster and stays engaged.


**Review together, regularly.** Set a recurring time — monthly works well — to sit down and look at the portfolio together. Ask your teen to explain why they bought what they bought and what they'd do differently now. That reflection habit is what separates investors from gamblers.


#### Track B: Young Adults Going Solo (Ages 18–24)


At 18, your young adult can open a self-directed brokerage account in their own name. Your role shifts from co-investor to advisor.


**Encourage a written investment plan.** Before they put money in, ask them to write down three things: what they're investing for, how long they plan to leave the money invested, and how they'll handle a 20% drop in value. Writing it down creates accountability and reduces panic selling when markets get rough.


**Introduce index funds early.** A low-cost ETF tracking a broad market index is a sensible starting point for most young adults. It's not exciting, but it's a foundation. Once they have a core position they understand, they can explore individual stocks or theme-based portfolios from a more stable base.


**Let them make mistakes.** At 18, a bad trade with a small amount of money is a cheap education. Resist the urge to intervene every time a position moves against them. Your job now is to be available for questions, not to manage the portfolio for them.

### Frequently Asked Questions


**What age can my teenager start investing?**
In the United States, teens under 18 need a custodial account set up by a parent or guardian. Some platforms, including Bloom, support teen accounts starting at age 13. At 18, your child can open a self-directed account independently.


**Do I need to be an experienced investor to teach my teen?**
No. You need to understand the basics — what stocks and ETFs are, how risk works, and why starting early matters. Apps like Bloom that include structured lessons can fill in the gaps for both of you as you go.


**How much money should a teenager start with?**
There's no universal right answer, but starting with a small amount — somewhere between $25 and $100 — is usually enough to make the experience feel real without creating anxiety over losses. Fractional shares mean even a small amount can be spread across multiple companies.


**What if my teen loses money?**
Losses are part of investing, and a small early loss is one of the most effective teachers available. The key is to review what happened together, understand why the position moved against them, and treat it as information rather than failure. This is exactly why starting with small amounts matters.


**Is it safe to let my teenager invest in real stocks?**
With a custodial account, you maintain oversight and can monitor what your teen is doing. The risk is market risk — the value of investments can go down. That's real, but it's manageable when position sizes are small and the focus is on learning. No investment is guaranteed to grow in value.


---


### Start the Conversation This Week


The best time to teach your teenager about investing is before they need the knowledge, not after. The 2026 Schwab survey data makes clear that your teen is already interested and already trusts you on this topic. That window doesn't stay open forever.


Pick one concept from this guide, bring it up at dinner, and see where the conversation goes. When you're ready to move from conversation to action,[Bloom](https://bloomapp.com/) gives you and your teen a structured place to start — for free.
